# Security policy

**Policy id:** `securemailscope-default` &nbsp;&nbsp; **Version:** `1.0.0` &nbsp;&nbsp; **Published:** 2026-09-21

This document is the human-readable form of the policy the assessment
engine applies.

A policy is a set of **choices**, not a set of forensic facts. Changing it
changes the judgement and never the observations: the reconstructed sessions,
handshakes and certificates in a report are identical whatever policy was
applied. That separation is the point of having a named, versioned policy at
all -- a reader who disagrees with a threshold can see exactly which one,
change it, and re-run against the same evidence.

## What the outcomes mean

| Outcome | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `FAIL` | The condition the rule tests for **was observed**. |
| `PASS` | Enough evidence was present to evaluate the condition, and it held. |
| `UNKNOWN` | The rule applies, but the capture does not contain what it needs. |
| `NOT_APPLICABLE` | The rule does not apply to this session at all. |

`UNKNOWN` is load-bearing and is never promoted to `PASS`. A capture that does
not show a certificate chain has not shown a *good* chain; it has shown
nothing. Only `FAIL` results become findings, so an unavailable observation
never produces one.

## Severity, confidence and priority are three axes

**Severity** is how bad the condition is under this policy. **Confidence** is
how sure we are the condition was observed. **Priority** is the ordering that
follows from both, plus any operator-supplied asset criticality.

They are never multiplied together. A `CRITICAL` finding seen with `LOW`
confidence stays `CRITICAL`; multiplying it by a confidence percentage would
quietly turn it into something that reads like a `MEDIUM`, presenting a
judgement about evidence quality as though it were a judgement about severity.
Priority comes from a lookup table, reproduced in
[scoring-methodology.md](scoring-methodology.md).

## Thresholds and why they are what they are

**`minimum_tls_version`** -- TLS 1.2 (0x0303). RFC 9325 §3.1.1 states TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1 MUST NOT be used, and NIST SP 800-52r2 §3.1 requires TLS 1.2 support. TLS 1.2 is NOT treated as a failure merely because TLS 1.3 exists: both are acceptable under this policy, and the rule assesses the negotiated configuration.

**`minimum_rsa_bits`** -- 2048 bits. RFC 9325 §3.2 and NIST SP 800-52r2 both place the floor for general-purpose RSA at 2048 bits, corresponding to roughly 112-bit security in NIST SP 800-57 Part 1 Rev. 5.

**`minimum_ec_bits`** -- 224 bits. NIST SP 800-57 Part 1 Rev. 5 places the minimum curve size for 112-bit security at 224 bits; secp256r1 and larger satisfy it.

**`deprecated_signature_hashes`** -- MD5 and SHA-1. RFC 9155 deprecates both for TLS signatures because practical collisions exist.

**`minimum_coverage_for_score`** -- 0.50. A score computed from less than half the applicable policy weight describes too little to be useful, so below this the engine reports SCORE_UNAVAILABLE rather than a number that looks authoritative. The value is a project judgement about readability, not a measured threshold.

**`score_bands`** -- STRONG >= 90, ADEQUATE >= 70, WEAK >= 40, CRITICAL below 40. Project-defined reading aids for the numeric score; they are not an industry classification and carry no external meaning.

**`severity_weights`** -- CRITICAL 10, HIGH 6, MEDIUM 3, LOW 1, INFO 0. Chosen so one CRITICAL control outweighs three MEDIUM ones. An ordering judgement, not a measurement, and fully configurable.

## Cipher policy

### Algorithms this policy will not accept

Each prohibited algorithm is owned by exactly **one** rule. Ownership is
what stops a single misconfigured setting being reported three times at
three severities.

| Algorithm | Reason | Reported by |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `NULL` | provides no confidentiality at all | `TLS-CIPHER-001` |
| `RC4_128` | RFC 7465 prohibits RC4 in TLS; practical keystream biases break it | `TLS-CIPHER-003` |
| `RC4_40` | export-grade RC4: a 40-bit key is brute-forceable | `TLS-CIPHER-003` |
| `DES_CBC` | single DES has a 56-bit key and is brute-forceable | `TLS-CIPHER-003` |
| `DES40_CBC` | export-grade DES: a 40-bit key is brute-forceable | `TLS-CIPHER-003` |
| `RC2_CBC_40` | export-grade RC2: a 40-bit key is brute-forceable | `TLS-CIPHER-003` |
| `3DES_EDE_CBC` | 64-bit block cipher vulnerable to birthday attacks (Sweet32) | `TLS-CIPHER-004` |

### Algorithms this policy approves

`AES_128_CCM`, `AES_128_CCM_8`, `AES_128_GCM`, `AES_256_GCM`, `CHACHA20_POLY1305`

All five are AEAD constructions. CBC-mode suites are **not** prohibited --
they are reported at `MEDIUM` under `TLS-CIPHER-005` as "not on the approved
list", because RFC 9325 §4.2 recommends AEAD rather than forbidding CBC. The
distinction between a prohibition and a recommendation is preserved
deliberately: see *Citation kinds* below.

## Severity weights

| Severity | Weight |
| --- | --- |
| CRITICAL | 10 |
| HIGH | 6 |
| MEDIUM | 3 |
| LOW | 1 |
| INFO | 0 |

These are **project-defined ordering judgements, not validated industry
benchmarks**. They were chosen so that one `CRITICAL` control outweighs three
`MEDIUM` ones, and so `INFO` contributes nothing to the score while remaining
reportable. Every one is configurable, and any change an operator makes is
recorded in the report's policy block and changes the policy fingerprint.

## Citation kinds

Every standards reference carries a `kind`, because conflating the three
is how "NIST says you must" claims get made about things NIST merely
recommends:

| Kind | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `PROTOCOL_REQUIREMENT` | The cited document requires this of conforming implementations. |
| `STANDARDS_RECOMMENDATION` | The cited document recommends it for general use. |
| `PROJECT_POLICY` | This project's own choice, cited as such. |
| `ENVIRONMENT_CHOICE` | Depends on the deployment; the operator decides. |

Rules sharing a **de-duplication group** describe one underlying weakness.
Scoring counts the group once and reports it once, charging the most severe
member that failed. A NULL-cipher session is therefore not penalised separately
for also being off the approved list.

## Rule detail

### `TLS-PROTO-001` -- Negotiated TLS version below the policy minimum

The version the server actually selected is older than the policy allows. Evaluated on the negotiated version only: a client offering an obsolete version that the server did not select is a separate, informational rule.

- **Applies when:** The session carries TLS and a version was negotiated.
- **Requires:** `A ServerHello establishing the negotiated version`
- **Technical impact:** Obsolete protocol versions lack modern AEAD constructions and carry known weaknesses in their record and handshake design, so traffic protected by them is easier to attack than traffic protected by TLS 1.2 or 1.3.
- **Remediation:** `REM-TLS-VERSION`
- **STANDARDS_RECOMMENDATION:** RFC 9325 §3.1.1 -- SSL/TLS Protocol Versions -- TLS 1.0 and 1.1 MUST NOT be used (2022-11)
- **STANDARDS_RECOMMENDATION:** NIST SP 800-52 Rev. 2 §3.1 -- Protocol Version Support -- TLS 1.2 required, TLS 1.3 recommended (2019-08)

### `TLS-PROTO-002` -- Client offered a protocol version below the policy minimum

The client advertised an obsolete version in its ClientHello. This is informational: it says nothing about what was negotiated, and a server that correctly refuses the obsolete version is behaving properly.

- **Applies when:** A ClientHello was observed.
- **Requires:** `A ClientHello listing offered versions`
- **Technical impact:** A client willing to use an obsolete version may be downgraded by an attacker able to influence negotiation, if the server also accepts it.
- **Remediation:** `REM-TLS-VERSION`
- **STANDARDS_RECOMMENDATION:** RFC 9325 §3.1.1 -- SSL/TLS Protocol Versions -- TLS 1.0 and 1.1 MUST NOT be used (2022-11)

### `TLS-PROTO-003` -- TLS negotiation ended in a fatal alert

A fatal alert was observed in plaintext, so the handshake did not complete. The cause is recorded from the alert description; no intent is inferred.

- **Applies when:** The session carries TLS.
- **Requires:** `A plaintext alert record`
- **Technical impact:** A failed negotiation means no protected channel was established for this session. Whether the client then fell back to plaintext is a separate observation.
- **PROTOCOL_REQUIREMENT:** RFC 5246 -- The Transport Layer Security (TLS) Protocol Version 1.2 (2008-08)

### `TLS-CIPHER-001` -- Negotiated cipher suite provides no encryption

The negotiated suite uses NULL encryption, so application data travels in the clear despite a TLS handshake having taken place.

- **Applies when:** A cipher suite was negotiated and is in the registry.
- **Requires:** `A ServerHello naming the selected cipher suite`
- **Technical impact:** Anyone able to capture the traffic can read it. The handshake provides integrity and authentication at best, and no confidentiality.
- **Remediation:** `REM-TLS-CIPHER`
- **STANDARDS_RECOMMENDATION:** RFC 9325 §4.1 -- General Guidelines on cipher suites (2022-11)

### `TLS-CIPHER-002` -- Negotiated cipher suite provides no server authentication

An anonymous suite was negotiated, so the server presented no certificate and its identity was never established.

- **Applies when:** A cipher suite was negotiated and is in the registry.
- **Requires:** `A ServerHello naming the selected cipher suite`
- **Technical impact:** Without server authentication the channel can be terminated by any party in the network path, so encryption alone does not establish who the peer is.
- **Remediation:** `REM-TLS-CIPHER`
- **STANDARDS_RECOMMENDATION:** RFC 9325 §4.1 -- General Guidelines on cipher suites (2022-11)

### `TLS-CIPHER-003` -- Negotiated cipher suite uses a prohibited cipher

The policy prohibits the negotiated encryption algorithm outright: RC4, export-grade ciphers and single DES all have practical attacks.

- **Applies when:** A cipher suite was negotiated and is in the registry.
- **Requires:** `A ServerHello naming the selected cipher suite`
- **Technical impact:** The encryption can be broken with resources well within reach of a motivated attacker who has recorded the traffic.
- **Remediation:** `REM-TLS-CIPHER`
- **STANDARDS_RECOMMENDATION:** RFC 9325 §4.1 -- General Guidelines on cipher suites (2022-11)

### `TLS-CIPHER-004` -- Negotiated cipher suite uses a 64-bit block cipher

3DES has a 64-bit block size, which makes long-lived connections vulnerable to birthday-bound collision attacks (Sweet32).

- **Applies when:** A cipher suite was negotiated and is in the registry.
- **Requires:** `A ServerHello naming the selected cipher suite`
- **Technical impact:** An attacker who can observe a very large volume of traffic on one connection can recover repeated plaintext blocks.
- **Remediation:** `REM-TLS-CIPHER`
- **STANDARDS_RECOMMENDATION:** RFC 9325 §4.1 -- General Guidelines on cipher suites (2022-11)

### `TLS-CIPHER-005` -- Negotiated cipher suite is not on the policy-approved list

The suite is not prohibited, but its encryption algorithm is not among those the policy approves. RFC 9325 §4.2 recommends AEAD suites; CBC-mode suites reach this rule rather than a prohibition rule.

- **Applies when:** A cipher suite was negotiated and is in the registry.
- **Requires:** `A ServerHello naming the selected cipher suite`
- **Technical impact:** Non-AEAD constructions have historically required careful implementation to avoid padding-oracle and timing attacks; AEAD removes that class.
- **Remediation:** `REM-TLS-CIPHER`
- **STANDARDS_RECOMMENDATION:** RFC 9325 §4.2 -- Cipher Suites for TLS 1.2 -- forward secrecy required (2022-11)

### `TLS-CIPHER-006` -- Negotiated cipher suite is not in the code-point registry

The selected suite's numeric identifier is not one this build knows, so its cryptographic properties cannot be assessed. Reported UNKNOWN, never guessed from the shape of a name.

- **Applies when:** A cipher suite was negotiated.
- **Requires:** `A registry entry for the selected cipher suite`
- **Technical impact:** An unassessable suite is an evidence gap, not a weakness. It may be perfectly strong or unacceptable; this capture does not say.
- **PROJECT_POLICY:** SecureMailScope assessment policy -- Project-defined default weighting and thresholds (2026-09-21)

### `TLS-KEX-001` -- Negotiated key exchange does not provide forward secrecy

The key establishment method the session negotiated has no ephemeral contribution, so a later compromise of the long-term key decrypts this recorded session. Covers static RSA key transport, static DH/ECDH and TLS 1.3 PSK-only resumption.

- **Applies when:** A key exchange method was established.
- **Requires:** `A negotiated key exchange method, from the cipher suite (TLS 1.2) or the key_share and PSK extensions (TLS 1.3)`
- **Technical impact:** An attacker who records the traffic now and obtains the server's long-term key later -- by compromise, legal compulsion or key reuse -- can decrypt the recorded session retrospectively.
- **Remediation:** `REM-TLS-FS`
- **STANDARDS_RECOMMENDATION:** RFC 9325 §4.2 -- Cipher Suites for TLS 1.2 -- forward secrecy required (2022-11)
- **PROTOCOL_REQUIREMENT:** RFC 5246 §7.4.7.1 -- RSA-Encrypted Premaster Secret Message -- static RSA key transport (2008-08)
- **PROTOCOL_REQUIREMENT:** RFC 8446 §2.2 -- Resumption and Pre-Shared Key -- psk_ke vs psk_dhe_ke (2018-08)

### `TLS-KEX-002` -- Hybrid post-quantum key-exchange group negotiated

The negotiated group combines a classical and a post-quantum algorithm. Recorded as an observation only: this assessment does not verify the post-quantum component's security properties and makes no claim about them.

- **Applies when:** TLS 1.3 was negotiated with an observable key_share.
- **Requires:** `A server key_share naming a hybrid group`
- **Technical impact:** Informational. A hybrid group is intended to remain secure if either component holds, but this tool observes only that one was selected.
- **PROTOCOL_REQUIREMENT:** RFC 8446 -- The Transport Layer Security (TLS) Protocol Version 1.3 (2018-08)
- **PROJECT_POLICY:** SecureMailScope assessment policy -- Project-defined default weighting and thresholds (2026-09-21)

### `CERT-001` -- Certificate had expired at the assessment reference time

The end-entity certificate's notAfter had passed. Judged at the capture timestamp in historical mode, which is the only way to say what was true when the traffic happened.

- **Applies when:** A certificate was observed in plaintext.
- **Requires:** `A decoded certificate and a reference timestamp`
- **Technical impact:** Clients enforcing validity reject the connection; clients that do not lose the assurance the expiry date exists to provide.
- **Remediation:** `REM-CERT-RENEW`
- **PROTOCOL_REQUIREMENT:** RFC 5280 §4.1.2.5 -- Validity -- notBefore and notAfter (2008-05)

### `CERT-002` -- Certificate was not yet valid at the assessment reference time

The end-entity certificate's notBefore had not been reached, which usually indicates a clock or provisioning error rather than expiry.

- **Applies when:** A certificate was observed in plaintext.
- **Requires:** `A decoded certificate and a reference timestamp`
- **Technical impact:** Conforming clients reject the certificate, and the mismatch suggests the server or its issuer has an incorrect clock.
- **Remediation:** `REM-CERT-RENEW`
- **PROTOCOL_REQUIREMENT:** RFC 5280 §4.1.2.5 -- Validity -- notBefore and notAfter (2008-05)

### `CERT-003` -- Certificate public key is below the policy minimum strength

The subject public key is smaller than the policy allows. Algorithms with fixed parameters, such as Ed25519, are NOT_APPLICABLE rather than failed.

- **Applies when:** A certificate was observed and its key has a variable size.
- **Requires:** `A decoded certificate with a describable public key`
- **Technical impact:** A key below the policy floor offers less work factor than the policy requires against an attacker attempting to recover it.
- **Remediation:** `REM-CERT-KEY`
- **STANDARDS_RECOMMENDATION:** RFC 9325 -- Recommendations for Secure Use of Transport Layer Security (TLS) and Datagram Transport Layer Security (DTLS) (2022-11)
- **STANDARDS_RECOMMENDATION:** NIST SP 800-52 Rev. 2 -- Guidelines for the Selection, Configuration, and Use of TLS Implementations (2019-08)

### `CERT-004` -- Certificate signature uses a deprecated hash

The certificate is signed with MD5 or SHA-1, for which practical collisions exist, so the signature no longer binds the certificate contents reliably.

- **Applies when:** A certificate was observed and its signature hash is known.
- **Requires:** `A decoded certificate naming its signature hash`
- **Technical impact:** An attacker able to construct a hash collision can produce a second certificate that the same signature appears to authenticate.
- **Remediation:** `REM-CERT-SIGALG`
- **STANDARDS_RECOMMENDATION:** RFC 9155 -- Deprecating MD5 and SHA-1 Signature Hashes in TLS 1.2 and DTLS 1.2 (2021-12)

### `CERT-005` -- Certificate chain verification failed

Path validation was attempted against a configured trust store and did not succeed. This rule fires ONLY on a verified failure: an unverified chain -- no trust store configured -- is UNKNOWN, not a failure.

- **Applies when:** A certificate was observed and chain verification was attempted.
- **Requires:** `A configured trust store and a completed path validation attempt`
- **Technical impact:** The presented certificate cannot be traced to a trusted issuer, so it provides no assurance about who the server is.
- **Remediation:** `REM-CERT-CHAIN`
- **PROTOCOL_REQUIREMENT:** RFC 5280 §6 -- Certification Path Validation (2008-05)

### `CERT-006` -- Certificate does not name the expected server identity

The certificate's subjectAltName entries do not match the identity the operator supplied. Fires ONLY on a verified mismatch: with no reference identity the rule is UNKNOWN, because there is nothing to compare against.

- **Applies when:** A certificate was observed and hostname verification ran.
- **Requires:** `An operator-supplied expected identity and a completed comparison`
- **Technical impact:** A client that checks names will refuse the connection; one that does not may be talking to a different service than intended.
- **Remediation:** `REM-CERT-IDENTITY`
- **PROTOCOL_REQUIREMENT:** RFC 6125 §6 -- Representation and Verification of Application Service Identity (2011-03)

### `CERT-007` -- End-entity certificate does not permit server authentication

The certificate carries an extendedKeyUsage extension that omits serverAuth. When the extension is absent, RFC 5280 leaves the certificate unconstrained, so the rule is UNKNOWN rather than failed.

- **Applies when:** A certificate was observed and declares an EKU.
- **Requires:** `A decoded certificate carrying an extendedKeyUsage extension`
- **Technical impact:** Clients enforcing EKU reject the certificate for TLS server authentication, and the certificate is being used outside its stated purpose.
- **Remediation:** `REM-CERT-EKU`
- **PROTOCOL_REQUIREMENT:** RFC 5280 -- Internet X.509 Public Key Infrastructure Certificate and CRL Profile (2008-05)

### `MAIL-001` -- Credentials submitted over an unencrypted email session

An authentication command was observed on a session where no TLS upgrade was ever accepted, so the credentials travelled in the clear. The credential itself is never recorded; only that an attempt occurred.

- **Applies when:** A plaintext email protocol was identified from payload.
- **Requires:** `An observed authentication command with no accepted TLS upgrade in effect`
- **Technical impact:** Anyone able to observe the network path obtains working mailbox credentials. Whether they did so is not something a capture can show.
- **Remediation:** `REM-MAIL-TLS-BEFORE-AUTH`, `REM-MAIL-ENABLE-STARTTLS`
- **STANDARDS_RECOMMENDATION:** RFC 8314 §3 -- Cleartext Considered Obsolete: Use of TLS for Email Submission and Access (2018-01)
- **STANDARDS_RECOMMENDATION:** RFC 9325 §3.2 -- Strict TLS -- use of TLS for mail submission and access (2022-11)

### `MAIL-002` -- Credentials submitted before the TLS upgrade took effect

An authentication command was observed before an upgrade that the server later accepted, so those credentials were exposed even though the session was eventually protected.

- **Applies when:** A plaintext email protocol was identified and an upgrade occurred.
- **Requires:** `An authentication command preceding an accepted upgrade boundary`
- **Technical impact:** The later upgrade does not protect what was already sent; those credentials should be treated as disclosed.
- **Remediation:** `REM-MAIL-TLS-BEFORE-AUTH`
- **STANDARDS_RECOMMENDATION:** RFC 8314 §3 -- Cleartext Considered Obsolete: Use of TLS for Email Submission and Access (2018-01)
- **PROTOCOL_REQUIREMENT:** RFC 3207 -- SMTP Service Extension for Secure SMTP over Transport Layer Security (2002-02)

### `MAIL-003` -- Opportunistic TLS upgrade was refused by the server

The client asked to upgrade and the server declined. Recorded as an observation of the server's configuration; no attack is inferred, since a refusal is also what a server without TLS configured legitimately does.

- **Applies when:** A plaintext email protocol was identified.
- **Requires:** `An upgrade command and a refusing server response`
- **Technical impact:** The session continues without transport protection, so everything after the refusal is readable on the path.
- **Remediation:** `REM-MAIL-ENABLE-STARTTLS`, `REM-MAIL-IMPLICIT-TLS`
- **PROTOCOL_REQUIREMENT:** RFC 3207 -- SMTP Service Extension for Secure SMTP over Transport Layer Security (2002-02)
- **STANDARDS_RECOMMENDATION:** RFC 8314 §3 -- Cleartext Considered Obsolete: Use of TLS for Email Submission and Access (2018-01)

### `MAIL-004` -- Upgrade accepted but TLS establishment was not observable

The server agreed to begin TLS and no TLS record framing follows in this capture. That is most often a capture artefact rather than a failure, which is why the severity is low and the limitation is stated explicitly.

- **Applies when:** An upgrade was accepted.
- **Requires:** `An accepted upgrade response and the bytes that follow it`
- **Technical impact:** This capture does not establish that the protected channel was actually set up. It is equally consistent with the capture simply ending.
- **PROTOCOL_REQUIREMENT:** RFC 3207 -- SMTP Service Extension for Secure SMTP over Transport Layer Security (2002-02)

### `MAIL-005` -- Plaintext email protocol continued after the upgrade was refused

After the server declined to upgrade, the client carried on issuing protocol commands in the clear rather than stopping.

- **Applies when:** An upgrade was refused on an identified email session.
- **Requires:** `A refused upgrade followed by further plaintext commands`
- **Technical impact:** Mail transactions, recipient lists and any credentials that follow are exposed on the network path.
- **Remediation:** `REM-MAIL-TLS-BEFORE-AUTH`, `REM-MAIL-ENABLE-STARTTLS`
- **STANDARDS_RECOMMENDATION:** RFC 8314 §3 -- Cleartext Considered Obsolete: Use of TLS for Email Submission and Access (2018-01)

### `MAIL-006` -- No opportunistic TLS mechanism was advertised

The server's capability response on a plaintext email session did not offer STARTTLS or STLS. This is an observation about the advertised configuration; it is NOT evidence of a stripping attack, which this tool cannot establish.

- **Applies when:** A plaintext email protocol was identified and capabilities seen.
- **Requires:** `A parsed server capability advertisement`
- **Technical impact:** Clients that would have upgraded have no way to do so, so the session stays in the clear.
- **Remediation:** `REM-MAIL-ENABLE-STARTTLS`, `REM-MAIL-IMPLICIT-TLS`
- **STANDARDS_RECOMMENDATION:** RFC 8314 §3 -- Cleartext Considered Obsolete: Use of TLS for Email Submission and Access (2018-01)
- **PROTOCOL_REQUIREMENT:** RFC 3207 -- SMTP Service Extension for Secure SMTP over Transport Layer Security (2002-02)

### `MAIL-007` -- Implicit TLS observed without an assessable negotiation

The session is TLS-framed from its first byte but the handshake was not observed well enough to assess the negotiated parameters. Reported UNKNOWN: the transport may be perfectly configured, and this capture does not say.

- **Applies when:** The session is TLS from its first byte.
- **Requires:** `An observable ServerHello on an implicit-TLS session`
- **Technical impact:** An evidence gap, not a weakness. A longer or earlier capture would resolve it.
- **STANDARDS_RECOMMENDATION:** RFC 8314 §3 -- Cleartext Considered Obsolete: Use of TLS for Email Submission and Access (2018-01)

## Limitations of this policy

- This policy encodes choices, not forensic facts. Changing it changes the judgement and never the underlying observations, which are reported unmodified alongside it.
- RFC 9325 and NIST SP 800-52 Rev. 2 are recommendations for general use. This project does not claim every recommendation in them is universally mandatory.
- The weights and score bands are project-defined initial values, not validated industry benchmarks.

See [limitations.md](limitations.md) for the limitations of the system as
a whole, and [scoring-methodology.md](scoring-methodology.md) for what the
